extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, and editors aiming to improve concise, correct English prose
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and recommendations for clear, concise, and correct English prose, covering sentence-level principles, matters of form (punctuation, quotations, numerals), and commonly misused words/expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit needless words
rubrics_metrics.description: Vigorous writing is concise: sentences and paragraphs should contain no unnecessary words or sentences; make every word tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make all sentences short, but remove redundancy (examples: 'the question as to whether' -> 'whether'; 'there is no doubt but that' -> 'no doubt'). Revise phrases like 'the fact that' (e.g., 'owing to the fact that' -> 'since'). Prefer positive statements and active voice. Combine related clauses to avoid step-by-step repetition (Macbeth example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a succession of loose sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write paragraphs made up of a series of similar loose sentences joined by simple conjunctions (and, but, so) or nonrestrictive relative clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such series become monotonous and weak. Recast sentences as simple sentences, semicolon joins, periodic sentences, or varied clause structures to remove sing-song rhythm. (Newspaper concert paragraph contrasted with better prose.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Express co-ordinate ideas in similar form (parallel construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of similar content and function should have similar outward form to make likeness of content clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parallel grammatical constructions for coordinated items and correlative expressions (both...and, not only...but also, either...or). Apply article/preposition repetition consistently (e.g., 'the French, the Italians, the Spanish, and the Portuguese'). Classify large lists into groups or use tables if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep related words together
rubrics_metrics.description: Position words and groups that are related in thought next to one another to show their relationship clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid separating subject and principal verb with transferably movable phrases; place relative pronoun immediately after its antecedent; put modifiers next to the words they modify (examples: 'Wordsworth gives a minute description' vs 'In the fifth book... Wordsworth gives...'). Exceptions: relative clauses in apposition and deliberate periodic sentence suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: In summaries, keep to one tense
rubrics_metrics.description: When summarizing, use a single tense throughout: present tense for drama and preferably for poems/stories/novels (past allowed), and keep antecedent actions consistent with perfect/past perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using present, express earlier actions with the perfect; if past, use past perfect for antecedents. Don't shift tenses arbitrarily. When summarizing others' speech or writing, indicate at the outset that what follows is summary and avoid repeated 'he said' tags; avoid long summaries in criticism—prefer orderly discussion with evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place emphatic words at the end
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the word or group you want to emphasize at the end of the sentence (or paragraph/composition) for prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The emphasized element is usually the logical predicate (the new information). Beginning position can also create emphasis. Use periodic sentences to give prominence. Examples show reordering to place emphasis on the intended element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headings (manuscript form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave a blank line after the title or heading of a manuscript; on succeeding pages begin at the first line if using ruled paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clean spacing conventions so headings are visually separated and manuscripts are consistently paginated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerals (form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not spell out dates or other serial numbers; write them in figures or suitable Roman notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'August 9, 1918' or '9 August 1918'; 'Rule 3'; 'Chapter XII'; '352nd Infantry.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses (punctuation rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence containing a parenthetical expression is punctuated as if the parenthesis were absent; the expression within is punctuated as if it stood alone, except omit the final period unless it is a question or exclamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a wholly detached sentence is parenthesized, place the final stop before the closing parenthesis. Examples: 'I went to his house yesterday (my third attempt to see him), but he had left town.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations (form and punctuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal documentary quotations are introduced by a colon and enclosed in quotation marks; quotations grammatically in apposition or as direct objects are preceded by a comma and enclosed in quotation marks; full lines of verse begin on a fresh centered line without quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations introduced by 'that' are indirect and not enclosed in quotes. Proverbial phrases and familiar literary phrases need no quotation marks; same for colloquialisms and slang.

rubrics_metrics.name: References (scholarly practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: In scholarly work, abbreviate frequently occurring titles (give full forms in an alphabetical list); give references in parentheses or footnotes rather than in-body; omit words like act, scene, line, book, volume, page unless needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punctuate references as indicated (examples: 'In III.ii', 'IV.ii. 14', '_2 Samuel_ i:17-27', '_Othello_ II.iii. 264-267').

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllabication (hyphenation at line breaks)
rubrics_metrics.description: When dividing words at the end of a line, divide according to formation, 'on the vowel', between double letters (with exceptions), and avoid dividing before a final -ed if the e is silent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative principles with examples: know-ledge, edi-ble, Apen-nines, treat-ed (not roam-ed). Consult examples and printed books to learn customary divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles (formatting literary titles)
rubrics_metrics.description: For titles of literary works, scholarly usage prefers italics with capitalized initials; omit initial 'A' or 'The' when placing a possessive before them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use italics except when writing for a periodical that follows a different practice. Examples: The _Iliad_; Dickens's _Tale of Two Cities_.

rubrics_metrics.name: All right (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'All right' is idiomatic in familiar speech as a detached phrase meaning 'Agreed' or 'Go ahead' but in other uses is better avoided; it is always written as two words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'all right' as two words; avoid it in formal writing unless used as the detached idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: As good or better than (construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'as good or better than' should be rearranged; 'My opinion is as good or better than his' is ambiguous/improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast to 'My opinion is as good as his, or better (if not better).' Choose clearer comparative constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: As to whether (redundancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Whether' is sufficient; do not use 'as to whether.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'whether' alone (see Rule 13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bid (verb usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Bid' takes the infinitive without 'to'; the past tense meaning 'ordered' is 'bade.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct complementation: 'bid him go' not 'bid him to go'; past 'bade' for 'ordered.'

rubrics_metrics.name: But (conjunction caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'But' is unnecessary after 'doubt' and 'help' and overuse of 'but' yields loose sentence problems and triteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions like 'I have no doubt but that' -> 'I have no doubt that'; prefer re-arrangement to avoid repetitive 'but' (example of two 'but's replaced by reordering sentences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Can (modal usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Can' means 'am/is/are able' and should not be used as a substitute for 'may.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'may' for permission/possibility where appropriate; use 'can' for ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case (redundancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'case' (meaning instance) is often unnecessary and can be replaced by a more direct phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'in many cases' with 'many of the rooms...' or restructure sentences to avoid 'it has rarely been the case that' -> 'few mistakes have been made.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainly (overuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Certainly' is often used indiscriminately as an intensifier (like 'very') and is a mannerism to avoid in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sparingly; avoid routine intensification that weakens prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (redundancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The noun 'character' is often redundant when 'hostile acts' or similar more direct phrasings will do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct terms: 'Hostile acts' instead of 'acts of a hostile character.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim (verb usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Claim' with an object-noun means 'lay claim to'; with a dependent clause it can be used if that sense is intended; do not use it as a substitute for 'declare', 'maintain', or 'charge'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'claim that' where 'lay claim to' fits; otherwise choose more precise verbs like 'assert' or 'maintain'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clever (overuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Clever' has been overused; restrict it to small-scale ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use more specific descriptors rather than 'clever' as a catch-all compliment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare to vs compare with
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Compare to' points out resemblances between different orders; 'compare with' points out differences between things of the same order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'compare to' for metaphoric likenesses (life compared to a drama) and 'compare with' for analytical comparisons (Congress compared with Parliament).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider (preposition usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'consider' means 'believe to be', it is not followed by 'as'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Say 'I consider him thoroughly competent.' Use 'consider...as' when meaning 'examine' ('considered Cromwell first as soldier...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Data (number agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Data' is plural and should take plural verbs (like 'phenomena', 'strata').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'These data were tabulated.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependable (word choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Dependable' is a needless substitute for 'reliable' or 'trustworthy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more direct, established synonyms when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different than (incorrect usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Different than' is not permissible; use 'different from', 'other than', or 'unlike'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'different from' for standard comparisons; adjust sentence structure if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divided into vs composed of
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Divided into' should not be misused for 'composed of'; e.g., plays are divided into acts, poems are composed of stanzas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between structural division and compositional makeup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't (contractions)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Don't' is the contraction of 'do not'; the contraction of 'does not' is 'doesn't'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contractions appropriately for register and grammatical clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due to (proper use)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Due to' is incorrectly used for 'through', 'because of', or 'owing to' in adverbial phrases; properly used when related as predicate or modifier to a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct: 'losses due to preventable fires.' Incorrect: 'He lost the first game, due to carelessness.' Use 'because of' or 'through' in adverbial contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folk (collective noun usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Folk' is a collective noun equivalent to 'people'; use the singular form only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'folk' as singular: 'folk is...' (author's note). Use 'people' for plural sense where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect vs affect (precision)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a noun, 'effect' means 'result'; as a verb, 'to effect' means 'to bring about'; do not confuse with 'affect' (to influence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague 'effects' in perfunctory writing about arts; prefer precise description of what is meant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etc. (usefulness and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Etc.' equals 'and the rest' and should not be used if omission would leave the reader uncertain about important particulars; at the end of a list introduced by 'such as' or 'for example' it is incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sparingly and only when it truly represents an obvious continuation; better to complete the list or rephrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (proper scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'fact' only for matters capable of direct verification; do not call matters of judgment 'facts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'the fact that' constructions where possible (see Rule 13). Example distinctions: dates and temperatures are facts; 'Napoleon was the greatest' is a judgment, not a fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (hackneyed word)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Factor' is overused; sentences using it can usually be rewritten more directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of 'His superior training was the great factor', write 'He won the match by being better trained.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature (hackneyed word)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Feature' often adds nothing to a sentence and is hackneyed; as a verb (advertising) it is to be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer specific description of the feature or tell what was sung/how she sang rather than 'a feature of the entertainment...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix (colloquial vs literary use)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Fix' in American colloquial use means 'arrange/prepare/mend' and should be restricted in writing to literary senses (fasten, make firm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'arrange', 'prepare', 'mend' in formal writing instead of colloquial 'fix'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get (colloquial registers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid colloquial 'have got' for 'have' in writing; participle 'got' preferred in formal register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'have' over 'have got' in formal prose; use 'got' as past participle where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: He is a man who (redundancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'He is a man who...' are commonly redundant; drop the extra clause and state directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'He is a man who is very ambitious' with 'He is very ambitious.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Help (redundant 'but' usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: See entry for 'But'—'help' followed by 'but' is unnecessary ('could not help see but that' -> 'could not help seeing that').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'help' constructions correctly: 'could not help seeing that.'

rubrics_metrics.name: However (position and meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'However' meaning 'nevertheless' should not begin its sentence or clause; when it comes first it means 'in whatever way' or 'to whatever extent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place 'however' mid-clause for 'nevertheless' ('At last, however, we succeeded...'). Use initial 'however' only for the 'in whatever way' sense ('However you advise him...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Interesting (avoid perfunctory label)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'interesting' as a perfunctory announcement; instead, make the story or point interesting by showing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't preface a story with 'An interesting story is told of'; simply tell the story without preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kind of / sort of (colloquial and vague)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'kind of' as a substitute for 'rather' (before adjectives/verbs) or for 'something like' except in familiar style; restrict it to its literal sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'rather' or 'something like' as appropriate; in formal writing avoid 'kind of' and 'sort of'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less vs fewer (count vs mass)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Less' should not be misused for 'fewer': 'less' refers to quantity, 'fewer' to number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'fewer' with countable nouns ('fewer men') and 'less' with mass nouns ('less water'); exceptions for round collective figures ('less than a hundred').

rubrics_metrics.name: Like vs as (usage with clauses)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Like' governs nouns and pronouns; before phrases and clauses the correct word is 'as'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'as' before clauses ('He thought as I did'; not 'He thought like I did'). 'Like' may replace 'as' only in informal registers with nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line, along these lines (cliché)
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'along these lines' is overworked and should be discarded for freshness; 'line' as 'course of procedure' is allowable but clichéd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clearer phrasing: 'to the same effect', 'He is studying French literature' instead of 'studying along the line of French literature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal, literally (avoid exaggeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'literally' incorrectly to support exaggeration or violent metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'literally' only when something is literally true: not 'a literal flood of abuse'; prefer 'a flood of abuse' or 'almost dead with fatigue' rather than 'literally dead'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lose out (colloquial redundancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Lose out' is a weak, overused intensifier compared with 'lose'; other '-out' and '-up' verbs may be idiomatic and distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simpler verbs unless the idiomatic phrasal verb conveys a distinct meaning (find out, run out, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Most (avoid for almost)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'most' to mean 'almost' (e.g., 'Most everybody' -> 'Almost everybody').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'almost' when that is the intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature (redundancy and vagueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Nature' is often redundant like 'character' and may be vaguely used (e.g., 'lover of nature' without specificity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace with more specific descriptors ('natural scenery', 'rural life', etc.) or drop the redundant word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Near by (adverb/adjective distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Near by' as an adverbial phrase is not fully accepted; use 'near' or 'near at hand'. As adjective use 'neighboring'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'near' or 'near at hand' adverbially; use 'neighboring' adjectivally rather than 'near by'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oftentimes / ofttimes (archaic)
rubrics_metrics.description: These are archaic; use the modern 'often'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'oftentimes' and 'ofttimes' with 'often' in modern prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: One hundred and one (retain 'and')
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain 'and' in expressions like 'one hundred and one' in accordance with long-standing English usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'one hundred and one' rather than 'one hundred one'.

rubrics_metrics.name: One of the most (threadbare openings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid opening with 'One of the most...' as a threadbare and weak formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't start essays or paragraphs with such formulas; they are commonplace and unimpressive. Beware singular-verb agreement errors after this expression ('one of the ablest men that have').

rubrics_metrics.name: Participle for verbal noun (gerund possessive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the possessive with gerunds where the possessive makes the meaning clear ('Do you mind my asking a question?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast awkward participial constructions: 'Do you mind my asking' rather than 'Do you mind me asking.' If meaning is unaffected or meaning refers to the actor, possessive is safer.

rubrics_metrics.name: People vs the people (political term)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The people' is a political term distinct from 'the public'; do not confuse them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'the public' when referring broadly to society rather than the political sense implied by 'the people'.
